item.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US.

Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.

Did Osmond realise how big he was back then? “You better believe it,” he says today. What was it like? “Incredible. Incredible.” In October 1973, a viewing balcony at Heathrow collapsed after fans went wild when Osmond and his brothers arrived in the country. Just after that, David Dimbleby hosted a debate on the BBC on teenage “hysteria”, asking whether the Osmonds were bad for the nation’s girls and if they should be deported. “My brother Alan said: ‘Donny, don’t forget this moment because nobody ever gets this!’” How did it make him feel? “I was enjoying every second of it. I was thinking this is so cool.”

Osmond was not deported. But in 1974, his solo career lurched to a sudden end. He continued having hits with his brothers for another year, then that all came crashing down, too. At 18, he was a pop has-been on two fronts. Osmond and his sister Marie reinvented themselves with a TV show, but ratings dropped after Osmond got married. The show was cancelled in 1979. By the age of 21, his career had gone kaput for a third time – and there appeared to be no coming back. It wasn’t simply that Osmond was no longer popular, but that somehow he had become an embarrassment. Even to himself.

And yet almost half a century on, Osmond has a Vegas residency six months a year, he released his 65th album a few years ago, and is about to embark on a tour of the UK. At 68, he is the father of five boys and a grandfather 16 times over. We meet in a London studio where he is having his photo taken. Today, he looks both distinctively Donny and, unsurprisingly, different. He’s got the slight body of a teenager and the monumental face of a Mount Rushmore president, giving him the air of a marionette. The hair is still bluey-black, the teeth pearly white. How does he manage it? “Well, as far as my hair is concerned, I have a lady who takes care of it. Her name is Clairol.” He pauses. “It’s a joke!” he says, patting my knee playfully. Osmond is one of life’s knee-patters. “I’d have grey sides if I didn’t take care of it. I’m not going to do that. But I’m really careful with what I eat. And I guess I was lucky in the DNA department. My mom had perfect skin.”

Has he had any plastic surgery? “No!” But, he says, there was a period when he tried Botox. “I hate it.” Why? He freezes his face into a rictus grin. “Nothing works. I tried it 15, 20 years ago. It took away my crow’s feet and I worked really hard for these crow’s feet.” He laughs.

Osmond, who is from Ogden, Utah, was five years old when he entered showbiz. There’s footage of him on the Andy Williams Show singing You Are My Sunshine. He was the youngest Osmond brother in the band at the time and clearly the standout, just as Michael was in the Jackson 5. It was an extraordinary period in music. The Beatles and the Rolling Stones, arguably the two greatest bands of all time, had spent the 60s fighting for supremacy. Now there were the Osmonds and the Jackson 5, the greatest boybands, battling it out. There was a perfect symmetry between them – five brothers, similar ages, with Donny and Michael both solo stars in their own right. The Jackson 5 were black, soulful and funky. The Osmonds were white, soulful and dabbled in hard rock. While Donny was initially the bigger solo star, the Jackson 5 had the edge on the Osmonds. They were a phenomenon, with their first four Motown singles going to No 1 on the US’s Billboard 100 in 1969 and 1970, a year before the Osmonds had their first hit.

Even now, more than 50 years on, Osmond seems to be restaging old battles with his great rivals and friends. He tells me he wants to set the record straight, and looks at me with the intensity of a man about to deliver an essential truth. “The Osmond brothers were the first boyband. People say: ‘No, it was the Beatles,’ but the Beatles were not a boyband. Then people say the Jackson 5.” And this is where it gets controversial. “We were before the Jackson 5. I’ll tell you a story.”

Osmond moves in closer to make his point. “The first time I met the Jackson 5, we were in Toronto performing and they were performing the next night. They flew in a day early to watch our show. I looked stage right and Michael was peeking around the corner watching me. But what happened afterwards was pretty darn amazing. We were in our hotel room and, Joe and Katherine [the Jacksons’ parents] were sitting on the sofa with my mom and dad. I can see it like it was yesterday.” He says each boy instinctively sought out their contemporary, from oldest to youngest. “So Jackie and Alan were talking, Wayne and Tito were talking, Jermaine and Merrill, Marlon and Jay.” Pause. “And Donny and Michael were nowhere to be found. Guess where we were?’’ He grins. “We were in the other room playing with our toys, trying to be kids. We were 13 or 14.” And did you manage to be kids? “Mike and I talked about it a lot. We both missed out on a childhood, but we agreed that we made up for it with the excitement of our lives.”…
